opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is one of the more striking things we've seen in the surveys. We ask essentially the same question two ways: some people get "in what year will there be a 10%, 50%, 90% chance of this milestone?" and others get "what's the probability of this happening by 10 years from now, 20 years, 50 years?" The fixed-years framing consistently produces later forecasts, sometimes by a lot, decades in some cases.

My honest answer is that I'm not totally sure why, but I have some guesses.

One is a kind of anchoring on the numbers you're handed. If I give you a year like 2040 and ask for a probability, you're sort of starting from "how likely is it that this crazy thing happens by this specific, concrete date?" and that can feel low. A specific date makes it feel imminent and real, so people are reluctant to put a big number on it. Whereas if I hand you "50%" and ask for a year, you're reaching out into the future until it feels plausible, and the far future is vague enough that it gets there sooner than you'd expect.

Related to that, people tend to avoid extreme probabilities. If the years we offer span a wide range, people may compress their answers toward the middle, giving modest probabilities even for fairly distant dates. That drags the implied distribution later.

There's also probably some asymmetry in how a far-off year feels versus a probability. "2070" sounds like forever, a number like "30%" doesn't necessarily feel committal. So the two framings tap different intuitions.

The bigger lesson, I think, is less about which framing is right and more that people don't have stable, well-formed beliefs here. If you can shift the answer by decades just by flipping the question around, that tells you these forecasts are pretty noisy and heavily constructed in the moment. That's why we ask both ways and combine them, rather than trusting either one on its own.

r001.rationale: The response says respondents may treat the milestone as a “crazy thing” and give modest probabilities even for fairly distant dates, suggesting low probabilities across queried years.

r002.rationale: The response says that starting from a specified probability can lead people to reach plausibility sooner, but it does not say that accepting a high probability makes an extremely distant year less tempting.

fable-5.1.text:
So, honestly, the first thing to say is that I'm not sure. This is one of those effects that showed up really robustly in our surveys and I don't think anyone has a fully satisfying account of it. But I can tell you the stories I find most plausible.

The basic finding is that if you ask someone "what's the probability that AI can do X by 2040?" you get a smaller number than you'd infer from asking them "in what year is there a fifty percent chance AI can do X?" Same person, same question in principle, and the answers imply quite different timelines. The fixed-year framing gives you later dates, by something like a decade in some of our data, which is a pretty wild discrepancy for what should be the same belief.

One story is about what gets anchored. When you give someone a year, you've handed them a point in time, and I think it's natural to sort of imagine the world in that year and ask "does this seem like a world where that's happened?" And when you imagine 2040, it probably looks a lot like now in your head, because that's the only material you have to build it from. Things that haven't happened yet don't feel present in the picture, so you say the probability is low. Whereas if you give someone a probability and ask for a year, they're now thinking about a trajectory. They have to imagine progress continuing, and extrapolation tends to be more aggressive than snapshot-imagining.

Another story is just about where people's defaults sit. If you're uncertain and you're asked for a probability, there's a pull toward smallish numbers, because a big probability feels like a strong claim and a small one feels modest. If you're uncertain and asked for a year, there's no obvious "modest" year. You have to pick something, and maybe twenty years feels like a reasonable hedge, which is actually a much more confident claim than it feels like.

And there's a third thing, which is that people might just not be converting between these representations very well. They may not have a single coherent distribution in their head at all. They have a cloud of intuitions, and the question format determines which intuitions get pulled out. In that case neither framing is "the real belief," and the gap is telling you something about how unformed these views are rather than which one is right.

The uncomfortable implication is that you can't just pick the framing you like. We mostly ended up reporting both, and I think the honest reading is that expert forecasts here carry a lot more noise than any single number suggests. Which is itself informative, I think, if slightly dispiriting.

r001.rationale: The response says large probabilities can feel like strong claims and that imagining a fixed year can yield low probabilities, but it does not say that the milestone seems extraordinary or that this keeps probabilities low across different queried years.

r002.rationale: The response discusses assigning a year for a 50% chance, but does not suggest that accepting a high probability in a particular year makes extremely distant year choices less tempting.

astra-6.text:
My guess is that people anchor on whatever you give them in the question, and then don’t adjust enough. If you give someone a year, they imagine what could happen by that year and come up with a probability. If you give them a probability—say, a fifty percent chance—they start thinking about a year that feels like a plausible time for that event. Those seem to be quite different mental processes, even though, in principle, they should give you consistent answers.

For a milestone that feels very uncertain or far away, I suspect the fixed-year question makes it easy to say, “Well, probably not by then.” Whereas asking for a year pushes you to construct a scenario in which it happens and put that somewhere on the calendar. But that’s a speculative explanation. The discrepancy is clearer than our understanding of what causes it, and it’s a reason to be cautious about treating these forecasts as precise measurements of people’s beliefs.

r001.rationale: The response mentions low probabilities for uncertain or far-away milestones, but does not say that an extraordinary milestone leads respondents to keep assigning low probabilities across different queried years.

r002.rationale: The response says that a specified probability prompts respondents to choose a plausible year, but does not suggest that accepting the milestone will reach a high probability makes an extremely distant year less tempting.

sol-6.1.text:
My guess is that the two framings draw your attention to different things. If I ask, “What’s the probability of this happening by 2050?” you might imagine the world in 2050 and consider all the obstacles to getting there. Whereas if I ask, “When will there be a 50 percent chance?” that somewhat takes for granted that it will happen, and your task is to find a date.

There could also be an anchoring effect. In the first case, you’re given a year; in the second, you have to generate one, and salient dates or familiar timelines might play a bigger role. But I don’t think we really know the explanation. What’s striking is that these are ways of asking for essentially the same information, and the framing seems to make a substantial difference.

r001.rationale: The response mentions considering obstacles in a queried year, but does not say that an extraordinary-seeming milestone keeps respondents assigning low probabilities across different years.

r002.rationale: The response says that asking when there is a 50% chance can make the milestone seem assumed, but does not say that accepting a high probability for a particular year makes an extremely distant year less tempting.
